title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
description: How model complexity trades off bias (underfitting) against variance (overfitting), and why total error is minimized at an intermediate complexity.
viz: interactive complexity slider showing training/test error curves diverge, with a fitted polynomial curve morphing from underfit to overfit on a scatter of data points

title: Bayes' Theorem
description: Prior, likelihood, and posterior — how Bayes' theorem updates beliefs given evidence, and its role in Naive Bayes, A/B testing, and calibration.
viz: interactive prior/likelihood sliders updating a live posterior distribution plot, plus a classic medical-test false-positive example

title: Central Limit Theorem
description: Why sample means of any distribution approach a normal distribution as sample size grows, and why this underlies confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.
viz: pick a skewed population distribution, draw repeated samples of size n, animate the histogram of sample means converging to a bell curve as n increases
gaps: Add the Law of Large Numbers in both forms — the weak LLN (the sample mean converges in probability to mu, provable from Chebyshev's inequality since Var(Xbar) = sigma^2/n -> 0) and the strong LLN (almost-sure convergence) — since the page currently mentions neither.

Draw the precise CLT-vs-LLN distinction the page cannot currently answer: the LLN says WHERE the sample mean lands (Xbar -> mu, a statement about the limit point), while the CLT describes the SHAPE and SCALE of the error around that limit (sqrt(n)(Xbar - mu) -> Normal(0, sigma^2), i.e. the error shrinks at rate 1/sqrt(n) and is asymptotically normal) — LLN gives consistency, CLT gives the confidence interval.

Add a worked <pre> code block that draws from a deliberately non-normal population (exponential, or a coin flip), takes many sample means at n = 2, 5, 30, and prints the mean and standard deviation of each sampling distribution next to the predicted sigma/sqrt(n) — turning the CLT from an assertion into a convergence the reader watches happen, and showing the sqrt(n) rate the LLN gap also asks about.

title: Hypothesis Testing & A/B Significance
description: Null vs alternative hypotheses, p-values, Type I/II errors, and statistical power — the machinery behind A/B test significance calls.
viz: two overlapping distributions (control vs treatment) with adjustable effect size and sample size, live p-value and power readout, shaded rejection region
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block computing the two-proportion z-test an A/B call actually rests on: pooled proportion, standard error sqrt(p(1-p)(1/n1+1/n2)), the z statistic and the two-sided p-value — then the sample-size-for-power inversion n = 2(z_{alpha/2}+z_beta)^2 p(1-p)/delta^2, so the reader can see why a 1% lift needs tens of thousands of users per arm.

title: MLE vs MAP Estimation
description: Maximum likelihood estimation vs maximum a posteriori estimation, and how a prior regularizes MLE — the probabilistic view of L2 regularization.
viz: adjustable prior strength slider showing the MAP estimate pull toward the prior mean away from the MLE point estimate on a likelihood surface

title: Linear Regression
description: Ordinary least squares, the normal equation, and gradient descent fitting a line — assumptions (linearity, homoscedasticity) and when they break.
viz: draggable data points with a live-fitted regression line and residual bars, plus a gradient descent path on the loss surface
gaps: State and explain the Gauss-Markov theorem and the BLUE (Best Linear Unbiased Estimator) property with its exact assumptions — linearity in parameters, strict exogeneity E[eps|X] = 0, homoscedasticity Var(eps|X) = sigma^2 I, no autocorrelation of errors, and no perfect multicollinearity — noting explicitly that normality of errors is NOT required for BLUE (only for exact t/F inference), and that 'best' means minimum variance among all LINEAR unbiased estimators.

Give the full derivation of the normal equation: write RSS(beta) = (y - X beta)^T (y - X beta), expand, take the gradient d RSS/d beta = -2 X^T y + 2 X^T X beta, set it to zero to get X^T X beta = X^T y, hence beta = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y, and note the Hessian 2 X^T X is positive semi-definite (so this is a minimum) and that the inverse fails exactly when columns are collinear.

Add a worked <pre> code block for the normal equation beta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y solved via lstsq or a QR/Cholesky factorisation rather than an explicit inverse, with a one-line note on why the explicit inverse is the numerically wrong habit when X^T X is ill-conditioned.

title: Logistic Regression
description: Sigmoid link function, log-odds, decision boundary, and maximum likelihood estimation for binary classification.
viz: 2D scatter with adjustable decision boundary driven by weight sliders, sigmoid curve showing probability output for a selected point
gaps: Explain why squared error composed with the sigmoid is non-convex in the weights: the (y - sigma(w^T x))^2 loss has a Hessian that changes sign because sigma'(z) = sigma(z)(1 - sigma(z)) vanishes in the saturated tails, so gradient descent can stall on plateaus or settle in a local minimum.

Show why log-loss / binary cross-entropy is the convex choice: -[y log p + (1-y) log(1-p)] with p = sigma(w^T x) has Hessian X^T diag(p_i(1 - p_i)) X, which is positive semi-definite for all w, so any stationary point is a global optimum — and the gradient simplifies to X^T (p - y).

Render the two loss surfaces side by side over the same weight for the same data so the MSE surface's flat saturated regions and bumps contrast with the cross-entropy bowl; the tokens 'MSE' and 'mean squared' currently appear zero times on the page.

Add a worked <pre> code block for the gradient of the log-loss, X^T (sigmoid(Xw) - y) / n, inside a gradient-descent loop — showing that the gradient has the same shape as linear regression's despite the nonlinearity, which is the fact that makes the algorithm memorable.

title: SVM & Maximum Margin
description: Maximum margin classifiers, support vectors, the kernel trick, and the C/gamma hyperparameters that control the margin-violation tradeoff.
viz: draggable 2D points forming two classes with live-computed max-margin hyperplane and support vectors highlighted, kernel selector morphing decision boundary
gaps: Add the explicit dual OBJECTIVE FUNCTION — maximize L_D(alpha) = sum_i alpha_i - (1/2) sum_i sum_j alpha_i alpha_j y_i y_j K(x_i, x_j) — which is currently absent even though the page already discusses Lagrangian duality, w = sum_i alpha_i y_i x_i, the box constraint alpha_i in [0, C], and the KKT conditions; do not restate that existing material, add the objective itself and note it is a concave quadratic program in alpha whose data dependence is only through inner products (hence the kernel trick).

Add the equality constraint sum_i alpha_i y_i = 0 (which arises from setting the derivative of the Lagrangian with respect to the bias b to zero) and connect it directly to the page's own SMO solver: SMO must update TWO multipliers simultaneously precisely because changing a single alpha_i alone would violate sum_i alpha_i y_i = 0, so the pair is moved along the line alpha_1 y_1 + alpha_2 y_2 = constant, clipped to the [0, C] box.

Add a worked <pre> code block for the hinge-loss objective max(0, 1 - y*f(x)) plus its subgradient update with the L2 term, and the kernel trick as a one-line substitution of K(x_i, x_j) for the dot product — the page discusses margins geometrically but never shows the loss being optimised.

title: Decision Trees
description: Recursive binary splitting, impurity measures (Gini, entropy), and how greedy splits build a tree — plus why deep trees overfit.
viz: animated recursive partitioning of a 2D feature space into rectangles as the tree grows, synced with the tree diagram building node by node
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for the greedy best-split search itself: loop over features, sort the column, scan candidate thresholds, compute the weighted child impurity (n_left/n * G_left + n_right/n * G_right) and keep the largest reduction. That loop is the whole algorithm and the page currently only describes it in prose.

title: k-Nearest Neighbors
description: Instance-based classification by majority vote among the k nearest neighbors, the curse of dimensionality, and the bias-variance effect of k.
viz: click to place a query point on a 2D scatter, k-slider highlighting nearest neighbors and live decision boundary changing shape as k changes
gaps: Replace the page's bare assertion that KNN fails in high dimensions with the actual distance-concentration mathematics: for i.i.d. dimensions, (Dmax(d) - Dmin(d)) / Dmin(d) -> 0 in probability as d -> infinity (Beyer et al.), so the nearest and farthest neighbours become indistinguishable and 'nearest' stops carrying information.

Give the underlying variance/mean argument that produces that result: for a squared distance that is a sum of d i.i.d. per-dimension contributions, the mean grows like O(d) while the standard deviation grows like O(sqrt(d)), so the relative spread sd/mean shrinks like O(1/sqrt(d)) and all pairwise distances concentrate around a single value.

Add the practical consequences that follow: the volume of a fixed-radius ball becomes a vanishing fraction of the space so any k-neighbourhood is no longer local, sample size must grow exponentially in d for constant density, and the fixes are dimensionality reduction, learned/supervised metrics, or cosine distance on sparse text.

Add a worked <pre> code block for the vectorised distance computation and top-k selection via argpartition rather than a full sort, plus distance-weighted voting — the O(n) query cost the page discusses only becomes concrete when the reader sees there is no training step at all.

title: Naive Bayes Classifier
description: Conditional independence assumption, how it simplifies Bayes' theorem for classification, and why it works well for text despite the naive assumption.
viz: spam/ham word-probability table with an interactive email example showing per-word likelihood contributions multiplying into a final posterior
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for multinomial Naive Bayes in log space: Laplace-smoothed likelihoods log((count_wc + alpha)/(total_c + alpha*V)), the log prior, and argmax over the summed logs — showing why the computation is done in logs (underflow on long documents) rather than by multiplying probabilities.

title: Bagging vs Boosting
description: Bootstrap aggregating (variance reduction via parallel models) vs boosting (bias reduction via sequential residual fitting) — the two ensemble philosophies.
viz: side-by-side animated panels: bagging training parallel trees on bootstrapped samples and averaging votes, vs boosting sequentially fitting trees to residuals

title: Random Forest
description: Bagging plus random feature subsampling — how decorrelating trees reduces variance further than bagging alone, and feature importance from impurity decrease.
viz: forest of small decision trees each trained on a bootstrap sample with a random feature subset highlighted, aggregating votes into a final boundary
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block showing the two independent sources of randomness together: the bootstrap row sample per tree AND the max_features column subsample drawn afresh at every split, then the majority vote. Also show the mean-impurity-decrease accumulation that produces the feature importances the page discusses.

title: Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM)
description: How XGBoost/LightGBM fit trees to the negative gradient of the loss, shrinkage (learning rate), and why boosting dominates tabular data leaderboards.
viz: iteration slider showing the ensemble prediction improving as successive trees are added, each fit to the current residual, with loss curve descending
gaps: Explain LightGBM's GOSS (Gradient-based One-Side Sampling) as the actual mechanistic answer to 'why is LightGBM fast': keep the top-a fraction of instances by absolute gradient, randomly sample a b fraction of the remaining small-gradient instances, and up-weight those sampled instances by (1-a)/b when computing information gain so the gain estimate stays unbiased.

Explain LightGBM's EFB (Exclusive Feature Bundling): sparse features that are rarely non-zero simultaneously (e.g. one-hot columns) are greedily graph-colored into bundles and packed into a single feature via offset ranges, cutting the effective feature count for histogram building.

Contrast LightGBM's leaf-wise (best-first, split the leaf with max delta-loss) growth against XGBoost's level-wise growth, including why leaf-wise gives lower loss per leaf but overfits small data and needs num_leaves / min_data_in_leaf control.

Present CatBoost's ordered boosting and ordered target statistics as a MECHANISM, not a product name: a random permutation of the rows, with each row's target-encoded value and gradient computed only from rows preceding it in that permutation, which removes the target leakage that plain mean target encoding and standard boosting's use of a row's own residual introduce.

Add a worked <pre> code block for one boosting round in the second-order formulation the page's math already uses: compute g_i and h_i for the current predictions, find the split maximising the gain, then set the leaf weight to -sum(g)/(sum(h)+lambda) and shrink it by the learning rate — tying the formula on the page to the loop that uses it.

title: Stacking Ensembles
description: Combining heterogeneous base models via a meta-learner trained on out-of-fold predictions — when stacking beats simple averaging.
viz: pipeline diagram: multiple base models producing out-of-fold predictions feeding into a meta-model, with a toggle comparing stacked vs averaged accuracy
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block building the out-of-fold prediction matrix with KFold before fitting the meta-learner, in that order. The ordering is the entire point — showing the leakage-free construction is what distinguishes stacking from naively training the meta-learner on in-sample base predictions.

title: k-Means Clustering
description: Centroid initialization, the assign-update Lloyd's algorithm loop, and the elbow method for choosing k.
viz: animated k-means iterations on a 2D point cloud showing centroids moving and cluster assignments recoloring each step, plus elbow plot for k selection
gaps: Add the explicit connection to Gaussian mixture models and EM: the assignment step is the hard-max of the EM E-step and the centroid update is the M-step mean update, so k-means is exactly the limiting case of EM on a GMM with equal mixing weights and spherical, tied covariance sigma^2 I as sigma^2 -> 0, where the soft responsibilities saturate to 0/1.

Use that limit to explain k-means' known failure modes mechanistically — assuming spherical, equal-size, equal-variance clusters means elongated or unequally-sized clusters get cut wrongly — and cross-reference the 39-gaussian-mixture-em concept for the soft-assignment generalization that fixes them.

Add a worked <pre> code block for the Lloyd iteration (assign to nearest centroid, recompute centroids as the cluster mean, repeat until assignments stop changing) alongside the k-means++ seeding that samples the next centroid with probability proportional to squared distance — the seeding is what makes the algorithm reliable and it is currently only named.

title: Hierarchical Clustering
description: Agglomerative clustering with linkage criteria (single, complete, average, Ward) and reading a dendrogram to choose cluster count.
viz: animated bottom-up merging of points into a dendrogram, with a draggable cut-height line showing resulting clusters on the scatter plot
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for the agglomerative merge loop: find the closest pair, merge, then update distances via the Lance-Williams recurrence for Ward linkage — which is how the dendrogram the page shows is actually built, and why Ward differs from single/complete linkage.

title: DBSCAN Density Clustering
description: Density-based clustering via core points, border points, and noise — eps/min_samples parameters and why DBSCAN finds arbitrary-shaped clusters k-means can't.
viz: adjustable eps radius and min_samples sliders on a 2D scatter with non-convex clusters, live core/border/noise point coloring
gaps: Present OPTICS as a mechanism rather than a name: it orders points by expanding a priority queue on reachability distance (max of a point's core distance and its actual distance to the expanding cluster), producing a reachability plot whose valleys are clusters and whose peaks are the boundaries between them, so a single run reveals clusters at many density levels and a chosen cut (xi steepness or a horizontal threshold) extracts a flat labelling.

Present HDBSCAN's full pipeline as a mechanism: mutual reachability distance d_mreach(a,b) = max(core_k(a), core_k(b), d(a,b)), building a minimum spanning tree in that metric, converting it to a hierarchy by removing edges in decreasing weight order, condensing the tree by requiring min_cluster_size so small splits become points falling out of a parent, and extracting a flat clustering by maximizing cluster stability (persistence summed over 1/lambda lifetimes).

Explain concretely why this handles variable density where DBSCAN cannot: DBSCAN's single global eps must be either too large (merging a sparse cluster into its neighbours) or too small (shattering the sparse cluster into noise) when clusters have different densities, whereas HDBSCAN selects a different effective eps per branch of the hierarchy and needs only min_cluster_size.

Add a worked <pre> code block for the region-query and cluster-expansion loop, with the three point roles (core, border, noise) assigned explicitly from the eps/minPts test — DBSCAN's ability to label a point as noise is its distinguishing feature and the code is where that becomes unambiguous.

title: Principal Component Analysis
description: PCA as variance-maximizing projection — eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, explained variance ratio, and dimensionality reduction tradeoffs.
viz: 2D point cloud with animated principal axes rotating to align with directions of max variance, scree plot of explained variance per component
gaps: Add kernel PCA as an actual mechanism, not a name: replace inner products with a kernel to get K_ij = k(x_i, x_j), center it in feature space with K_centered = K - 1_N K - K 1_N + 1_N K 1_N, eigendecompose K_centered, normalize each eigenvector alpha_k by 1/sqrt(lambda_k), and project a new point as sum_i alpha_ki k(x_i, x) — noting there is no explicit feature map and no simple inverse transform back to input space.

Add probabilistic PCA as a latent-variable model: x = W z + mu + eps with z ~ N(0, I) and isotropic Gaussian noise eps ~ N(0, sigma^2 I), giving marginal x ~ N(mu, W W^T + sigma^2 I); its maximum-likelihood solution recovers the top-q eigenvectors scaled by sqrt(lambda_i - sigma^2) with sigma^2 the average discarded eigenvalue, and it yields a likelihood for model selection, principled handling of missing data, and classical PCA as sigma^2 -> 0.

Add the Gram-matrix / dual trick for d >> n: eigendecompose the n x n matrix X X^T instead of the d x d covariance X^T X, since the two share non-zero eigenvalues and the principal directions map back via v = X^T u / sqrt(lambda), turning an O(d^3) problem into O(n^3) — the same duality that kernel PCA generalizes.

Add a worked <pre> code block computing PCA by SVD on the mean-centred matrix, with the explained-variance ratio from the singular values (s^2 / sum(s^2)) — plus a line on why SVD is preferred to forming the covariance matrix and eigendecomposing it, which squares the condition number.

title: t-SNE & UMAP

viz: high-dimensional cluster data projected to 2D with perplexity/n_neighbors slider reshaping the embedding, side-by-side with a linear PCA projection
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for the pieces the visualization already computes but the prose never shows: the sigma binary search targeting log2(k) perplexity, the t-conorm symmetrisation W = w + w^T - w*w^T, and the min_dist -> (a, b) curve fit that turns the low-dimensional kernel 1/(1+a||y||^{2b}) into a knob a reader can reason about.

title: Cross-Validation Strategies
description: K-fold, stratified, and time-series splits — how cross-validation estimates generalization error and avoids the single-split variance trap.
viz: animated k-fold rotation showing which fold is held out each round, aggregating per-fold scores into a mean plus-minus std bar
gaps: Cover preprocessing leakage explicitly: fitting a StandardScaler, imputer, target/ordinal encoder, or SelectKBest/RFE feature selector on the FULL dataset before splitting leaks test-set statistics into every training fold; demonstrate the inflated CV score this produces versus the honest one.

Introduce sklearn Pipeline / make_pipeline as the concrete fix — the literal token 'Pipeline' currently appears zero times on the page — showing that cross_val_score(make_pipeline(scaler, selector, model), X, y) refits every transform inside each training fold only, and that ColumnTransformer belongs inside the pipeline too.

Distinguish target leakage (a feature computed from the label or from information only available after the outcome) from train-test contamination (test rows influencing any fit), and state plainly that fit-before-split preprocessing leakage is the single most-tested cross-validation gotcha in interviews.

Add a worked <pre> code block showing the fold loop with the entire preprocessing pipeline fitted INSIDE the fold, next to the leaking version that scales or selects features before splitting. The page's argument is about leakage; the two versions side by side are what make the leak visible.

title: Confusion Matrix & Metrics
description: Precision, recall, F1, and specificity derived from the confusion matrix — how threshold choice trades off false positives against false negatives.
viz: draggable classification threshold on a probability histogram updating a live confusion matrix and precision/recall/F1 readout
gaps: Add the Matthews correlation coefficient with its formula MCC = (TP*TN - FP*FN) / sqrt((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)), its -1..+1 range, and why it is the most honest single-number summary under class imbalance: it is the only common metric that uses all four confusion-matrix cells, so it cannot be inflated by predicting the majority class.

Add Cohen's kappa, kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e) where p_o is observed agreement and p_e is agreement expected by chance from the marginals, as the chance-corrected agreement measure (also used for inter-annotator agreement on labels).

Add balanced accuracy as the unweighted mean of per-class recall — (sensitivity + specificity)/2 in the binary case — and contrast all three against plain accuracy on a worked 99:1 imbalanced example where a majority-class-only classifier scores 0.99 accuracy but 0.5 balanced accuracy and 0.0 MCC.

Add a worked <pre> code block computing the confusion matrix and deriving precision, recall, F1 and specificity from its four cells, then sweeping the decision threshold to show the precision/recall trade-off moving — the page presents the metrics as definitions but never as a function of the threshold the reader controls.

title: Learning Curves Diagnosis

Add human-level performance as the practical proxy for Bayes error when the true value is unknown (and the caveat that 'human-level' should mean expert or panel-of-experts performance, not average, for the proxy to be tight).

Add Andrew Ng's avoidable-bias vs variance decomposition as the actual decision rule the curve is read with: avoidable bias = train error - Bayes error (or its human proxy), variance = validation error - train error; if avoidable bias dominates, add capacity / train longer / better features (more data will NOT help, and show this as the flat converged-curve signature), and if variance dominates, add data, regularize, or augment.

title: Gradient Descent Variants
description: Batch, stochastic, and mini-batch gradient descent, plus momentum, RMSProp, and Adam — how each modifies the update rule to escape saddle points and speed convergence.
viz: optimizer selector racing SGD/Momentum/RMSProp/Adam simultaneously across a 3D loss surface with saddle points, showing each path's convergence speed
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block placing the update rules side by side — plain SGD, momentum, RMSProp, and Adam with its bias-correction terms m_hat = m/(1-beta1^t), v_hat = v/(1-beta2^t). Seeing the four updates in the same notation is what makes the family resemblance and the bias-correction's purpose obvious.

title: L1 vs L2 Regularization
description: L1 (Lasso) vs L2 (Ridge) penalties — why L1's diamond constraint region produces sparse weights while L2's circular region shrinks smoothly.
viz: adjustable lambda slider showing weight coefficients shrinking toward zero, with L1 constraint diamond vs L2 constraint circle overlaid on the loss contours
gaps: Add early stopping as implicit L2 regularization: for gradient descent with learning rate eta on a quadratic objective with Hessian eigenvalue lambda_i, after t steps the parameter along eigendirection i has been shrunk by a factor (1 - (1 - eta lambda_i)^t) relative to its unregularized optimum, which matches L2/ridge's lambda_i/(lambda_i + alpha) shrinkage — so the number of steps t plays the role of 1/alpha (few steps = strong regularization, many steps = weak).

Make the mechanism concrete: directions with large curvature are learned first and directions with small curvature stay near their initialization, so training time acts as an effective-parameter budget; illustrate with the training-time axis annotated as an inverse regularization-strength axis, and note this is why early stopping and weight decay are partly redundant.

Add a worked <pre> code block for the two gradient updates side by side — the L2 term 2*lambda*w against L1's lambda*sign(w) — and the soft-thresholding operator that drives a coefficient exactly to zero. That the L1 subgradient is constant regardless of magnitude is the whole reason sparsity happens.

title: Dropout & Batch Normalization

gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for inverted dropout (scaling by 1/(1-p) at train time so inference needs no rescaling) and batch-norm forward with its running mean/var buffers — both written to show the train-vs-eval branch explicitly, since forgetting that branch is the classic bug this page should inoculate against.

title: Backpropagation

viz: small feedforward network with animated forward pass (activations lighting up) followed by backward pass (gradient arrows flowing back), editable input to see gradients recompute
gaps: Add numerical gradient checking as the concrete debugging tool for a hand-written backward pass: the centered finite difference (f(theta + eps) - f(theta - eps)) / (2 eps) with eps around 1e-5..1e-7, which has O(eps^2) error versus the one-sided difference's O(eps).

Add the relative-error acceptance criterion |g_analytic - g_numeric| / max(|g_analytic|, |g_numeric|, tiny) with the usual thresholds (< 1e-7 good, ~1e-4 suspicious for shallow nets and only tolerable with kinks, > 1e-3 a bug), rather than comparing raw absolute differences.

Add the practical caveats: use float64 (float32 round-off alone can blow past the threshold), check only a random subset of parameters per tensor because the check costs two forward passes per parameter, turn off dropout and other stochasticity so both evaluations see the same function, and beware kinks — ReLU, max-pooling and the hinge/abs losses are non-differentiable at zero, so a perturbation that straddles a kink makes the numeric gradient legitimately disagree; test at points away from kinks or with fewer datapoints.

Add a worked <pre> code block for a full forward and backward pass over a two-layer network with the chain rule written out per layer, showing the cached forward activations being consumed by the backward pass — the caching is what makes backprop cheaper than numerical differentiation and it is invisible in prose.

title: Categorical Encoding
description: One-hot, ordinal, target, and embedding encodings for categorical features — the cardinality/leakage tradeoffs of each.
viz: categorical column with a selector cycling through encoding schemes, live-rendering the resulting feature matrix and flagging target-leakage risk
gaps: Add feature hashing (the hashing trick) as a distinct encoding: apply a hash function to the category string and take it modulo a fixed dimension m to get the index to increment, giving a fixed-width output for unbounded or streaming cardinality with no fitted vocabulary and no dictionary to store or update at serving time.

Explain collision behaviour concretely: two categories mapping to the same bucket share a weight, but because collisions are random and most categories are rare, the model degrades gracefully rather than failing — the expected number of colliding pairs falls as m grows, so m is the accuracy/memory dial; contrast this with one-hot's memory blowup and target encoding's need for a fitted mapping.

Add the signed-hash variant: multiply each increment by a second hash xi(x) in {-1, +1} so that collisions cancel in expectation, making the hashed inner product an unbiased estimator of the true one (the Weinberger et al. hashing-kernel result).

Add a worked <pre> code block for target encoding computed inside cross-validation folds with smoothing toward the global mean, next to the naive full-data version that leaks — plus one-hot and ordinal for contrast. Target encoding's leakage failure mode is the reason this page needs code rather than a table.

title: Handling Imbalanced Data
description: Class imbalance techniques — random oversampling, SMOTE, class weighting, and threshold tuning — and how each reshapes the decision boundary.
viz: adjustable class-imbalance ratio on a 2D scatter with a technique selector (none/oversample/SMOTE/class-weight) showing the resulting decision boundary shift
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block covering the three levers the page names: SMOTE's interpolation between a minority point and one of its k nearest minority neighbours, class_weight='balanced' as n/(k*n_c), and threshold selection from the precision-recall curve rather than a default 0.5 — showing they are alternatives, not a pipeline.

title: Recommender Systems
description: Collaborative filtering (user-based, item-based, matrix factorization) vs content-based filtering, and hybrid architectures used in production recommenders.
viz: user-item interaction matrix with animated matrix factorization into latent factors, plus a toggle between collaborative and content-based recommendation output
gaps: Add BPR (Bayesian Personalized Ranking) for implicit feedback: instead of regressing on missing-as-zero entries, sample triples (user u, observed item i, unobserved item j) and maximize sum log sigma(x_ui - x_uj) minus L2 regularization, i.e. a pairwise ranking loss that only requires i to be scored above j — and explain why this suits click/view data where absence is not a negative.

Add sequential and session-based recommendation as a distinct family: GRU4Rec running a recurrent net over the ordered interaction sequence with session-parallel mini-batches and a ranking loss, and SASRec-style causal self-attention over the interaction history that lets recent items dominate the next-item prediction — capturing order and intent that a static user-factor vector cannot.

Add multi-armed bandits as the exploration mechanism for cold start and feedback loops: epsilon-greedy, UCB, and Thompson sampling (sample from each arm's posterior, e.g. Beta over click-through rate, and serve the argmax), plus contextual bandits like LinUCB — framed as the fix for the popularity feedback loop where a recommender never learns about items it never shows.

Add a worked <pre> code block for matrix factorisation by alternating least squares or SGD over observed ratings only, with the regularised update, and the cold-start branch that falls back to content features — showing that the loss is summed over observed entries rather than the full matrix is the detail the page's diagram cannot convey.

title: A/B Testing for ML Products
description: Randomized experiment design for ML products — sample size/power calculation, novelty effects, and common pitfalls like peeking and Simpson's paradox.
viz: live A/B experiment simulator with adjustable traffic split and effect size, running sequential p-value tracking and flagging the 'peeking' false-positive trap
gaps: Add SUTVA (the stable unit treatment value assumption) and state precisely what it requires: one unit's outcome depends only on its OWN assignment, and there is a single version of the treatment — the assumption every standard A/B t-test silently relies on.

Add network and interference effects as the concrete SUTVA violation: in marketplaces a treated buyer consumes inventory a control buyer would have bought, in social graphs a treated user's posts reach control friends, and in two-sided platforms treatment and control compete for the same supply — all of which bias the measured effect (usually inflating it via cannibalization) no matter how large the sample.

Add the fixes as mechanisms: cluster/graph randomization (randomize whole social communities, cities, or markets so interference stays within an arm, at the cost of a much larger effective variance and a design effect of 1 + (m-1) rho requiring cluster-robust standard errors), and switchback / time-sliced randomization where the whole system alternates between treatment and control over time buckets for strongly interfering systems like pricing and dispatch, with a burn-in window per switch to absorb carryover.

title: Time Series Decomposition
description: Decomposing a time series into trend, seasonality, and residual components (additive vs multiplicative), and why decomposition guides model choice.
viz: time series chart with animated decomposition into trend/seasonal/residual layers, an additive/multiplicative toggle reshaping the seasonal component

title: ARIMA Forecasting
description: AR, I, MA components of ARIMA, stationarity and differencing, and reading ACF/PACF plots to choose model order.
viz: raw vs differenced series with live ACF/PACF plots, order (p,d,q) sliders regenerating an ARIMA forecast with a confidence band

title: Gaussian Mixture Models & EM
description: Mixtures of Gaussians fit by expectation-maximization — soft responsibilities instead of k-means' hard assignments, the E-step posterior and M-step closed-form updates, covariance types (full, tied, diagonal, spherical), and choosing the number of components by BIC/AIC.
viz: step-through E-step/M-step buttons on a 2D scatter of overlapping elongated clusters: the E-step recolors each point by blending the component colors in proportion to its soft responsibilities while the M-step redraws the covariance ellipses, a covariance-type selector (full/tied/diag/spherical) constrains the ellipse shapes, a running log-likelihood trace shows it never decreasing across iterations, a re-seed button lands the same data in a visibly worse local optimum, and a covariance-shrink slider collapses the ellipses to points so responsibilities harden to 0/1 and the fit becomes literal k-means

title: Probability Calibration
description: Making predicted scores behave like real probabilities — Platt (sigmoid) scaling vs isotonic regression and their data requirements, reliability curves, Brier score and its refinement/calibration decomposition, expected calibration error, and why resampling or class weighting for imbalance destroys calibration and forces a recalibration step.
viz: a reliability diagram with a bin-count slider and a model selector (logistic regression, random forest, boosted trees, SVM) showing the forest's S-shaped under-confidence at the extremes against the boosted tree's opposite bow, a calibration-method selector (none/Platt/isotonic) redrawing the curve toward the diagonal with live Brier and ECE readouts, a calibration-set-size slider shrinking until isotonic's step function visibly overfits and its held-out Brier worsens while Platt's holds, and an imbalance-handling toggle (none/SMOTE/class-weight) that visibly lifts the whole curve above the diagonal to show predicted probabilities inflated by resampling

title: Feature Importance & Interpretability
description: Explaining what a model learned — permutation importance, partial dependence plots with their feature-independence assumption plus per-instance ICE curves, SHAP values aggregated from local to global (and TreeSHAP), LIME and its instability across reruns, and the impurity/Gini importance bias toward high-cardinality features together with the fix.
viz: a fitted random forest on a dataset seeded with a pure-noise high-cardinality ID column, with a method selector (impurity/Gini, permutation on held-out data, drop-column, SHAP) re-sorting the importance bar chart so the useless ID column ranks first under impurity and collapses to zero under permutation, a correlation slider between two genuinely predictive features that visibly splits their importance in half as it rises, a PDP/ICE toggle overlaying the individual conditional expectation spaghetti on the averaged curve to expose an interaction the PDP hides, and a re-run LIME button producing a visibly different local explanation for the same point each press

title: Causal Inference Basics
description: Getting causal effects from observational data — confounding and why correlation is not causation, potential outcomes and counterfactuals, propensity score matching and inverse propensity weighting, difference-in-differences and its parallel-trends assumption, instrumental variables (relevance plus the exclusion restriction), regression discontinuity, and uplift modeling for who to treat.
viz: a simulated marketing dataset with a known ground-truth treatment effect and a confounder-strength slider that drags the naive difference-in-means away from the true value, an estimator selector (naive, propensity matching, IPW, difference-in-differences, instrumental variable) snapping the estimate back toward truth with its confidence interval, a propensity-overlap histogram that thins out and makes IPW weights explode as confounding grows, a draggable pre-period control trend that breaks parallel trends and visibly biases the DiD number, and an uplift panel sorting users into persuadables/sure-things/lost-causes/sleeping-dogs so targeting the top uplift decile beats targeting the top response-probability decile

title: Nested CV & Model Comparison Tests
description: Why reusing one cross-validation loop for both hyperparameter tuning and reporting gives an optimistically biased score, the nested inner-tuning/outer-evaluation structure and its k_inner x k_outer cost, and the statistical tests for declaring one model better — Dietterich's 5x2cv paired t-test, McNemar's test, DeLong's test for correlated AUCs, and multiple-comparison correction.
viz: side-by-side flat-CV and nested-CV simulators run on data where every candidate model is secretly identical, with a grid-size slider that inflates the flat loop's reported best score further above the honest outer-loop score as the grid grows (winner's-curse selection bias made visible) alongside a live model-fit counter showing nested CV's cost, plus a comparison panel where picking two classifiers runs the 5x2cv paired t-test, McNemar's test on the shared test set's discordant-pair table, and DeLong's test on the two ROC curves, printing each p-value beside a Bonferroni/Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected threshold that flips several 'significant' verdicts to non-significant as the number of compared models rises
